The two functions of a router

Routing happens at layer 3. A router performs two functions:

  • Determine the best path to the destination. For that it needs information about the network topology.
  • Switch the datagram: it receives it, checks its table, chooses an outgoing interface, encapsulates it in a layer 2 message and sends it.

The forwarding decision is made at each router, one after another, until the end is reached.
Each router decides only the next step; the full path is built hop by hop.

1 · Determine the best path
It checks its routing table: who do I pass this datagram to?

2 · Switch the datagram
It encapsulates it in a data link layer frame and sends it out the chosen interface.

Routers and all devices (a PC too) have a routing table: the structure where the information about which path to follow is gathered, sometimes detailed and sometimes summarized.

Each entry contains:

  • Destination network and mask.
  • Gateway: the next hop.
  • Interface used to reach that next hop.
  • Metric: a qualifier. If there are two possible entries, the one with the lower metric wins.
The table does not describe the whole path: it says who to pass the datagram to and through which interface.
Highlighted row: to reach network 192.168.0.0, traffic leaves through interface 192.168.0.12. The first row (0.0.0.0) is the default route: we will see it in a moment.
On-link: the destination is a neighbor

On-link in the Gateway column means the destination is a neighbor: it is on the same LAN, no intermediary is needed.

If A wants to communicate with 192.168.0.20, the 192.168.0.0 entry matches. A then runs ARP, finds out which station it is and delivers the frame to it directly.

This is possible precisely because it is a neighbor: ARP only works within the same LAN.
On-link = direct delivery: resolved with ARP, without going through a router.
Longest match: the longest match wins

Since each entry has a mask, the match with the destination is partial: only the bits the mask indicates are compared.

The IP module takes the destination IP and walks the table sequentially, because there is no exact match to look for.

If several entries match (for example, the same prefix with a different mask) the longest match one is always chosen: the one with the largest number of matching bits.
More matching bits = more specific information about where the destination is.
Destination 200.5.10.8: which entry matches in the most bits?
The default route and the default gateway

The 0.0.0.0 entry is the default route: it is always true and is the worst possible match. If the destination matches no other entry, it matches this one: it takes everything unknown.

Its gateway is the default gateway: a neighbor that allows leaving the network.

A wants to reach 200.5.10.8. It is not a neighbor, so only 0.0.0.0 matches and the datagram is passed to R1 (192.168.0.1).
When I don't know who to deliver the datagram to, I pass it to the default gateway.
At the router, everything starts again

The datagram arrives at R1 and the process starts over: it reads the destination IP, walks its table and chooses by longest match.

A router usually has multiple interfaces, so the decision is more complex than on a PC.

Then it switches: it builds a new layer 2 frame and sends the datagram out the chosen interface toward the next hop.

This passing from router to router is called a hop.
Every hop repeats the same thing: destination IP → table → outgoing interface.

This repeats at each router until the end, which happens in one of three cases:

  • A router determines that the destination is a neighbor: it delivers it directly (via ARP).
  • No path was found: the datagram cannot be delivered.
  • The packet reached the end of its lifetime (the TTL hit 0) and is discarded.

Here R2 has network 200.5.10.0 on-link: S is its neighbor.
The last router no longer looks for a gateway: it looks for the destination's MAC.
What is asked of a routing protocol

A routing protocol is an application that runs on the router. It is meant to be:

  • Flexible: it adapts quickly to topology changes.
  • Optimal: able to choose the best route.
  • Of fast convergence.
  • Robust: it operates despite possible failures.
  • Simple: it must not use up the router's resources (or links).

If a link goes down, the routers detect it and tell each other about the change: they are converging.
The protocol has converged when all routers have consistent routing tables.
While they notify each other of the change, they converge. When all agree on the possible paths, it has converged.

• Static / dynamic: routes written by hand or learned.
  • Single / multi-path: a single path, or several with load balancing.
  • Flat / hierarchical: everyone shares everything (does not scale), or areas that talk with a central area.
  • Interior / exterior: an IGP runs inside an organization; the exterior one connects organizations, showing only what they want.
  • Distance vector / link state: counts hops, or also evaluates bandwidth, delay and reliability.
The path with the fewest hops is not always the best: there may be a longer one with more bandwidth.
All the protocols in the course are interior (IGP). In the next lesson we look at the two highlighted ones: RIP and OSPF.

• The router determines the best path and switches the datagram.
  • Routing table: destination network, mask, gateway, interface and metric.
  • On-link: the destination is a neighbor, resolved with ARP.
  • Longest match wins; 0.0.0.0 takes the unknown and sends it to the default gateway.
  • Hop by hop until the destination is a neighbor, there is no route, or the TTL runs out.

Tables can be loaded by hand, but usually a protocol builds them. In the next lesson: RIP and OSPF.
Three tables, three decisions: A uses the default route, R1 finds a more specific entry and R2 has the destination as a neighbor.

A router has the entries 0.0.0.0 /0, 200.5.0.0 /16 and 200.5.10.0 /24. A datagram arrives for 200.5.10.8. Which one does it use?
200.5.0.0 /16, because it comes first in the table
200.5.10.0 /24, because it is the longest match
All three match, but the longest match is always chosen: the entry with the most matching bits, in this case the /24.
